title: AI writing: Present gains can weaken future judgment
desc: Supports supervised augmentation and independent competence assessment while emphasizing verification costs and lost developmental opportunities.

kps.k: The central dispute concerns what human contribution AI-assisted writing must preserve, not simply whether writers use AI.
kps.d: The Input Layer locates legitimate assistance in human analysis completed before AI execution. Anthea Roberts’s Extended Mind essay instead treats thinking and authorship as iterative co-creation, provided humans genuinely direct higher-level work. Jen Leonard reserves book drafting for herself while using AI for research and feedback. These positions support human agency but differ over whether generating prose forms an indispensable part of thinking or can be delegated without surrendering authorship.

qs.q: There’s another possibility that he doesn’t consider: you do the hard thinking first, all of it, the planning, the analysis, the strategy, the judgment, and then you bring in the AI to execute on that thinking, or to pressure-test it, or to help you see what you missed.
qs.a: The Input Layer: Prompt Engineering Isn't Dead. You're Just Doing It Wrong. · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: So when people ask the question "did you write it, or did the AI?", my reaction is that we both wrote it and that the framing of the question is wrong.
qs.a: The Extended Mind: Why Did You Do It or Did the AI? Is the Wrong Question · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Reported performance evidence supports conditional augmentation, not universal improvement.
kps.d: Applying AI to Rebuild Middle Class Jobs reports that Noy and Zhang’s 2023 writing study narrowed productivity gaps while preserving the strongest writers’ advantage. It also reports roughly 14% productivity gains and faster novice progression in Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond’s 2023 customer-service study. By contrast, Daniel Schwarcz describes legal-writing revision results in which stronger initial drafts deteriorated while weaker drafts improved. He labels fatigue, time pressure and excessive deference as speculative explanations. These findings concern different tasks and conditions; they do not establish that AI invariably strengthens or weakens expertise.

qs.q: While the best writers remained at the top of the heap using either set of tools, ChatGPT enabled the most capable to write faster and the less capable to write both faster and better — so the productivity gap between adequate and excellent writers shrank.
qs.a: Applying AI to Rebuild Middle Class Jobs · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Bridget McCormack: One of the interesting things about the study was that, during the revision phase, the stronger writers submitted poorer work when they were aided with AI, while the writers who didn’t start with a strong human draft actually improved.
qs.a: Can AI Make Lawyers Better? — Daniel Schwarcz · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Verification remains essential, but its cost and difficulty challenge the assumption that human oversight guarantees useful results.
kps.d: The Input Layer and You Should Be CentaurMaxxing warn that polished prose encourages unchecked reliance; their explanations of all hallucinated-citation incidents as professional abdication remain author interpretations. On Working with Wizards reports a confirmed error discovered by GPT-5 Pro in a published paper, yet leaves the model’s claimed analytical process unverified. It warns that checking sophisticated output can exceed either production time or the user’s expertise. The supplied D.C. Bar Opinion 388 discussion likewise recommends assessing net workload task by task. Successful generation, absence of detected errors and reliable final work remain distinct.

qs.q: The better AI gets at producing polished, confident, professional-looking output, the easier it becomes to trust the surface, to skip the verification, to let the packaging convince you.
qs.a: The Input Layer: Prompt Engineering Isn't Dead. You're Just Doing It Wrong. · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: I checked through the results, and found that it was, but I still have no idea of what the AI did to discover this problem, nor whether the other things it claimed to have done happened as described.
qs.a: On Working with Wizards · Market & press · 2025

kps.k: AI creates a developmental tension: delegating work may expand present capability while removing opportunities to acquire future judgment.
kps.d: Am I Cheating? and On Working with Wizards warn that polished output can conceal weak understanding, an undeveloped voice or missed practice. Roberts acknowledges reported cognitive-atrophy research but argues that reduced detailed recall can coexist with stronger strategic thinking, as in legal teams. The customer-service learning gains offer a counterpoint to inevitable deskilling, not proof of durable independent legal competence. The unresolved question is which workflows build understanding and which merely improve assisted output.

qs.q: There’s a difference between producing a polished draft with AI and deeply understanding how that draft came to be.
qs.a: Am I Cheating? Writing with AI and the Question of Authenticity · Academia · 2025

qs.q: And that suggests another risk we don't talk about enough: every time we hand work to a wizard, we lose a chance to develop our own expertise, to build the very judgment we need to evaluate the wizard's work.
qs.a: On Working with Wizards · Market & press · 2025

kps.k: Educational proposals pair supervised AI use with independent demonstrations of competence rather than choosing unrestricted adoption or blanket bans.
kps.d: Teaching Law in the Age of Generative AI proposes independent starting work, prompt records, reflective accounts and instructor assessment of the interaction process. Law School AI Bans Teach Exactly the Wrong Lesson supports restrictions tailored to instructional goals while arguing that students must practise scrutinising generated legal analysis. The O’Leary–Perlin episode supplies a concrete Suffolk example: AI modules alongside a planned three-hour closed-packet drafting final, plus oral briefings as a way to test understanding. These are pedagogical proposals and implementation accounts, not demonstrated learning-effectiveness results.

qs.q: Students can be required to “show their work,” providing the instructor with a record of prompts and a re- flection on how they incorporated AI-generated materials in their final product.
qs.a: Teaching Law in the Age of Generative AI · Academia · 2024

qs.q: But those are arguments for assignment-level rules, not an institution-wide default ban.
qs.a: Law School AI Bans Teach Exactly the Wrong Lesson · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Practical accounts favour selective delegation, but they do not establish a single optimal workflow.
kps.d: You Should Be CentaurMaxxing allocates routine drafting to AI while retaining consequential language and negotiation decisions. Leonard’s accounts distinguish useful planning, research and feedback from an unsuccessful attempt to accelerate difficult writing. Other speakers value reversible inline edits and simulated scholarly critique. Getting Your Hands Dirty argues that leaders must develop firsthand skill in context-setting, task decomposition and error detection. Client-reputation prompting and scholar-persona feedback remain personal techniques, not validated substitutes for legal expertise or human verification.

qs.q: It's not "use AI for everything." It's not "never use AI." It's a constant, task-level assessment of where AI adds value and where it doesn't, driven by domain expertise that the AI itself cannot provide.
qs.a: You Should Be CentaurMaxxing. · Law firms · 2026

qs.q: Eventually I realized that I'd just found all new tech-infused ways to procrastinate.
qs.a: GPT-5 and the Future of Legal AI Regulation — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Authenticity and professional identity remain contested even when output is useful or accurate.
kps.d: The E37 speakers report disengaging from perceived AI-written content, whereas Roberts and Forsyth question whether disclosed assistance necessarily constitutes cheating. The presentation of self in the age of ChatGPT interprets corrective editing and concealment as ways professionals preserve recognition, not as ethical recommendations. It also warns that augmentation can threaten employment when demand fails to expand with capacity. Generative AI and the Future of Legal Scholarship goes further: its author argues that inexpensive competent scholarship challenges the purpose of scholarly production itself. These identity, employment and institutional arguments rely largely on reflection, analogy and qualified predictions rather than measured displacement.

qs.q: Because as soon as I think this is not authentic, this is not them, it's someone else.
qs.a: E37 -  Zach and Richard’s Excellent Legal AI Adventure: Claude and the Legaltech Apocalypse · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: However, if you say upfront that you’re using an AI, are you really cheating in the classic sense?
qs.a: Am I Cheating? Writing with AI and the Question of Authenticity · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Institutional disagreement turns on whether to regulate AI’s involvement or the quality and accountability of the resulting work.
kps.d: A commenter on the Fifth Circuit proposal rejects AI-drafted submissions on the premise that predictive generation cannot constitute legal analysis; this is not the court’s position. Lawyers’ Monopoly and the Promises of AI instead favours existing Rule 11 verification duties and low-stakes comparative pilots over additional AI-specific bans or certifications. The presentation of self proposes provenance records and oversight attestations to make contribution visible, while acknowledging their signalling function. McCormack urges comparison with fallible human practice without excusing AI errors. The practical divide concerns what disclosure and restrictions add to substantive checking, independent competence and outcome-based evaluation.

qs.q: Do we really want parties to submit legal work product to courts drafted by a robot that can’t think?
qs.a: Fifth Circuit proposed Rule 32.3 and Form 6 (AI-use certification): notice, public comments, and the court's June 2024 decision not to adopt · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: I'm not sure that AI-specific bans or certifications add much (if anything) to Rule 11.
qs.a: Lawyers' Monopoly and the Promises of AI · Academia · 2025

vlens.an: The legal-tech vendor source neither accepts nor rejects the proposition that AI writing’s present gains can weaken future judgment. It focuses on descriptive, task-level adoption: lawyers may already use AI without counting it as such, familiar writing tools may overlap functionally with newer generative AI, and assistance with drafting or concision may encourage broader experimentation. This is compatible with the cluster’s recognition of selective augmentation, but it provides no position on the proposition’s decisive conditions and risks—human supervision, verification costs, independent competence assessment, lost developmental opportunities, or whether assisted performance builds durable judgment. Internal variation is limited to different aspects of practical use rather than competing views on those issues: one strand reframes existing ChatGPT use as adoption, while another compares writing tools and describes curiosity-driven expansion. Because this evidence comes from one curated source, it should not be treated as representative of legal-tech vendors generally.

qs.q: You guys talk about two tools that are so different in theory, but are doing the exact same thing.
qs.a: From Legacy Machine Learning to Generative AI · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: And I agree, getting started writing the pieces really hard, getting more concise, and going to that, the curiosity starts getting further, right?
qs.a: From Legacy Machine Learning to Generative AI · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

vlens.an:
The curated academia-and-research sources broadly accept the proposition’s core: AI-assisted writing can deliver immediate gains, but those gains depend on active human judgment, verification and preserved opportunities to demonstrate independent competence. Collectively, they materially develop that proposition through concrete educational designs, performance evidence and accountability mechanisms. Proposed approaches include assignment-specific rather than blanket restrictions, independent work before AI consultation, assessment of students’ prompts and reflections, oral briefings, closed-packet drafting examinations, low-stakes comparative pilots, provenance records and attestations of human oversight.

The common reasoning is that fluent output is not equivalent to understanding or reliable work. Reflective sources warn that delegating drafting can conceal weak mastery, inhibit development of voice or reduce cognitive engagement; practical and pedagogical sources therefore emphasise learning to direct, interrogate, edit and verify generated work. Empirical claims are more qualified: reported studies indicate that AI can narrow skill gaps and accelerate novice performance, while Schwarcz’s legal-writing experiment found that AI-assisted revision improved weaker drafts but worsened stronger ones under constrained conditions. This supports conditional, task-specific augmentation rather than universal improvement, although proposed explanations involving fatigue and excessive deference remain explicitly speculative.

Material internal variation concerns what must remain human and how serious developmental loss is. Some sources treat struggling through prose as part of learning to think; Roberts instead argues that writing is not indispensable to thinking and that selective tactical offloading may strengthen higher-level strategic cognition, provided the human genuinely performs that higher-level work. Several sources focus primarily on education and verification, while others extend the issue to authorship, professional identity, employment and institutional accountability. One source redirects the debate toward the purpose of legal scholarship once competent output becomes nearly costless, and the online-labour-market excerpt establishes writing’s exposure to GPT without taking a position on judgment, verification or competence. These differences do not amount to an overall rejection of the proposition. The evidence base also varies substantially—from experiments and reported studies to implementation accounts, personal practice, analogy and prediction—so developmental and institutional claims should not be treated as uniformly demonstrated findings, nor this curated set as representative of academia generally.

qs.q: To reduce overreliance on AI, students could begin each step of the process on their own before turning to the AI for additional insights.
qs.a: Teaching Law in the Age of Generative AI · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Bridget McCormack: One of the interesting things about the study was that, during the revision phase, the stronger writers submitted poorer work when they were aided with AI, while the writers who didn’t start with a strong human draft actually improved.
qs.a: Can AI Make Lawyers Better? — Daniel Schwarcz · Academia · 2026

vlens.an: This curated set of market-analyst, consultancy and press voices accepts the proposition’s core case for selective, supervised augmentation and materially develops its account of why oversight may fail. Common reasons include the risk that polished output invites misplaced trust, the need to preserve human analysis and task-level judgment, and concern that delegation removes practice needed to develop the expertise used in verification. There is material internal variation: The Input Layer permits AI execution after humans complete the underlying thinking; the E37 speakers take a stricter authenticity-based position against AI-written published articles while allowing limited brainstorming; and On Working with Wizards is more receptive to autonomous AI’s speed and sophistication but argues that opaque processes can make verification costly or impossible and can weaken future evaluative judgment. These claims rest largely on professional reflection and personal trials, including one confirmed error-detection case, rather than general evidence of durable deskilling.

qs.q: The better AI gets at producing polished, confident, professional-looking output, the easier it becomes to trust the surface, to skip the verification, to let the packaging convince you.
qs.a: The Input Layer: Prompt Engineering Isn't Dead. You're Just Doing It Wrong. · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: And that suggests another risk we don't talk about enough: every time we hand work to a wizard, we lose a chance to develop our own expertise, to build the very judgment we need to evaluate the wizard's work.
qs.a: On Working with Wizards · Market & press · 2025

vlens.an: This anonymous frontline-practitioner account supports the proposition’s model of selective, supervised augmentation. The practitioner reports substantial value from rapid drafting frameworks, preliminary issue analysis and medical-record timelines, but treats these outputs as starting points rather than filing-ready legal work. The principal reasons are that generated case citations may be fabricated, case-law analysis can fail, most generated drafting requires replacement, and even apparently accurate summaries demand entry-by-entry human verification. The account also directly raises the developmental risk that junior lawyers may lose opportunities to build independent judgment. Its internal variation is between strong enthusiasm for speed and structure and deep scepticism about reliability and reasoning: AI can provide a useful analytical head start without being trustworthy enough for autonomous reliance. The reported accuracy and productivity figures are personal estimates, not systematic evidence, and this single curated anonymous account should not be treated as representative of frontline practitioners generally.

vlens.an: These selected traditional-law-firm sources support the proposition’s core preference for selective, supervised AI augmentation rather than wholesale adoption or rejection. Their common rationale is that AI can take on routine or low-risk work while lawyers retain the contextual judgment and expertise needed to direct, revise and verify it. Material variation lies in evidential strength and emphasis: the Quinn Emanuel discussion relies on prediction and an anecdote about brainstorming, stressing transferable communication skills but not verification costs or developmental loss; “You Should Be CentaurMaxxing.” offers a more developed risk-based workflow and warns that polished output can conceal errors requiring expert verification. Neither source substantively examines whether delegation weakens future judgment or proposes independent competence assessment, so the professional voice supports rather than materially extends the full synthesis. Because the corpus is curated, this position should not be treated as representative of traditional law firms generally.

qs.q: It's not "use AI for everything." It's not "never use AI." It's a constant, task-level assessment of where AI adds value and where it doesn't, driven by domain expertise that the AI itself cannot provide.
qs.a: You Should Be CentaurMaxxing. · Law firms · 2026

qs.q: And as these models get better at producing polished work, the trap gets harder to see, not easier—AI makes mistakes in ways that require real expertise to catch.

vlens.an: Within this curated selection, the professional voice broadly accepts the proposition’s case for supervised, selective AI augmentation. The common rationale is that humans must retain responsibility for framing the task, exercising judgment, approving or reversing edits, and verifying the final work; several accounts also reserve drafting or initial thinking for the human because cognitive effort contributes to learning and quality. The D.C. Bar material adds that verification may offset generation-time savings and that AI-generated support can carry little persuasive weight when inadequately substantiated. Material internal variation remains: a Fifth Circuit commenter rejects AI-drafted court submissions categorically because predictive generation is not, in that commenter’s view, legal analysis, while Jen Leonard elsewhere redirects attention from preserving cognitively rewarding tasks toward professional purpose and better outcomes. Other favourable accounts are narrower and experiential, demonstrating user-controlled editing, planning, research and feedback without establishing long-term effects on independent competence. These selected records therefore support the proposition overall, but do not show a uniform institutional position or supply systematic evidence for every claimed developmental risk.

qs.q: - [A]ll results and content need careful inspection for accuracy, some tweaking or deep edits — and both tech companies advise users to verify everything generated by the AI.“I don’t want people to abdicate responsibility,” said Kristina Behr, vice president of product management for collaboration apps at Google Workspace.
qs.a: D.C. Bar Ethics Opinion 388: Attorneys' Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Client Matters · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: But if you're working on a project where your goal really is to learn about the content and develop new ideas and new connections, you want your brain to be deeply invested in that learning process.

elens.an: The curated 2023–2024 sources overall support the proposition’s model of conditional, supervised augmentation. Their common reasoning is that generative AI can produce immediate writing and productivity gains, but useful reliance still depends on human expertise, task-specific verification and retained user control. Reported studies add important nuance: AI narrowed writing-skill gaps and accelerated novice customer-service performance, indicating that developmental loss is not inevitable, while stronger performers retained an advantage. The clearest material development comes from legal education proposals that preserve independent initial work, require validation, and assess students’ interaction with AI rather than only the finished product. Internal variation is substantial. Some favourable accounts are first-person demonstrations rather than measured evidence; one employment source establishes writing’s near-term applicability but does not address judgment or development; a Fifth Circuit commenter categorically rejects AI-drafted briefs because predictive generation is not legal analysis; and Jen Leonard redirects attention from preserving intellectually rewarding work toward professional purpose and outcomes. These exceptions do not displace the period’s broader support for supervised use, but they show disagreement over whether safeguards make AI-assisted writing acceptable and whether preserving traditional writing work is itself the right objective. Because the corpus is curated, this synthesis describes the supplied sources and does not establish the prevalence of these views among authors, lawyers or institutions.

qs.q: So as you do each task, you may want to consider whether AI will save you time or actually create more work.
qs.a: D.C. Bar Ethics Opinion 388: Attorneys' Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Client Matters · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: To reduce overreliance on AI, students could begin each step of the process on their own before turning to the AI for additional insights.

elens.an: The curated 2025 sources accept the cluster’s principal proposition that AI-assisted writing should be selective and human-supervised, with verification and independent competence preserved. They materially develop it in three ways: first, they explain the circular developmental risk that delegation can remove the practice needed to acquire the judgment required for verification; second, they show that verification may be costly or impossible when outputs or claimed processes exceed the user’s expertise; and third, they propose concrete institutional responses, including oral briefings, closed-packet drafting examinations, provenance records and attestations of human oversight. Common reasons for this position are that AI can provide useful planning, critique, structure and rapid first-pass work, but polished output is not equivalent to understanding or reliable final work. Material variation remains over how much drafting can safely be delegated, whether existing duties such as Rule 11 are preferable to AI-specific requirements, and whether assistance affects authorship, professional identity or employment as well as competence. One source merely documents everyday use and expanding experimentation without addressing these safeguards, so its relation is unclear. Claims of productivity, deskilling and adoption at scale are mostly anecdotal, reflective or predictive in this period; the sources do not establish a universally optimal workflow or measured long-term loss of competence.

qs.q: And that suggests another risk we don't talk about enough: every time we hand work to a wizard, we lose a chance to develop our own expertise, to build the very judgment we need to evaluate the wizard's work.
qs.a: On Working with Wizards · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: For instance, at Suffolk we’ve embraced AI – we’re integrating Hotshot’s legal AI modules into the first-year fall curriculum, we’re doing an exercise on AI outputs and prompting and all the things – but for the first time in a while, our students will take a closed-book legal writing final in December with just their brain, their fingertips, their laptop, and a closed packet of materials.
qs.a: How AI Is Changing Legal Education with Dyane O'Leary and Jonah Perlin — full episode transcript · Academia · 2025

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources overall support the proposition that AI writing should be selectively supervised, verified and paired with preserved human competence rather than adopted indiscriminately or prohibited wholesale. Common reasons include the risk that polished output encourages misplaced trust, evidence that AI assistance can improve weaker work while worsening stronger work under some conditions, and the need to allocate tasks according to risk, context and the user’s expertise. Educational sources accordingly favour supervised practice plus assignment-specific restrictions, while practical accounts retain consequential judgment, drafting or final review for humans. There is material internal variation over what must remain human: some require analysis before AI execution; Roberts permits iterative co-creation if the human genuinely performs higher-level thinking; Leonard and the E37 speakers reserve authorship or published drafting more strictly. Schwarcz adds conditional performance evidence rather than assuming universal gains, and Getting Your Hands Dirty extends the proposition by arguing that leaders need firsthand practice to develop supervisory judgment. One legal-scholarship source redirects from workflow safeguards to the institutional purpose of scholarship once competent-looking output becomes extremely cheap. These positions describe this curated set only and do not establish their prevalence among 2026 commentators.

qs.q: The first time our students critically evaluate an AI-generated legal analysis should be in a classroom, where the stakes are a grade and the feedback comes from a professor, not in practice, where the stakes are a client’s liberty or livelihood and the feedback comes from a sanctions order.
